MESSAGE:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?

REQUESTS:
1. Suggest a name for the delivery van
2. Work out the drop order and timeline meeting all time windows, the break and the 12:00 return  KEY: Only feasible order is B -> A -> C. Leave 08:30, arrive B 08:50, unload to 09:05 (done before 09:30); arrive A 09:30, unload to 09:45 (inside 09:00-10:00); arrive C 10:25, wait until 11:00 (take the 30-min break during this wait); unload 11:00-11:15; back at depot 12:00 exactly (zero slack). A-first fails (B reached 09:40, after opening). Must give order B, A, C with a timeline that respects all constraints.
3. Rewrite the delivery text to be friendlier
4. List three furniture checks before handover
5. Recommend paper vs emailed delivery note
6. Define 'proof of delivery' in a line
7. Draft an evening-before arrival text under 160 characters

ANSWER:
## Van name ideas

- **Chester Drawers**
- **Vincent Van Go**
- **The Dovetail**
- **Sideboard Sid**
- **Veneer Far Away**
- **French Polish Express**

My vote is Chester Drawers.

## Tomorrow's route: **B → A → C**

This is the **only order that works**:
- **A or C can't go first.** If you start at A, the earliest you can finish there is 09:15. Driving on to B gets you there at 09:40, after the shop opens. C can't be visited before 11:00, so it can't come before B either.
- **That leaves B → A → C.**

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive B, unload |
| 09:05 | Finish at B ✅ (25 min before opening) |
| 09:30 | Arrive A, unload ✅ (within the 09:00–10:00 window) |
| 09:45 | Finish at A |
| 09:45–10:15 | **30-minute break** |
| 10:15 | Drive to C |
| 10:55 | Arrive C, wait 5 min |
| 11:00 | Unload at C ✅ |
| 11:15 | Leave C |
| 12:00 | **Back at depot** ✅ |

The break can be taken anywhere in the gap between A and C, for example near C from 10:25 to 10:55 instead.

**⚠️ There is no slack on the return.** C can't start before 11:00 and the drive back takes 45 minutes, so the van gets back at exactly 12:00. No change of route can improve this. If anyone at C keeps the driver waiting even a few minutes, he'll be late back. Call C today and ask them to have someone ready to receive the delivery at 11:00 sharp. Also tell the depot that a return of up to about 12:10 is possible.

## Friendlier "on the way" text

> Hi [Name], [Driver] from [Business] is on his way with your furniture and should be with you in about [X] minutes. See you soon!

## Evening-before text (141 characters)

> Hi Sarah, your furniture from Oakline Restoration arrives tomorrow 9-11am. We'll text when we're on our way. Any problems? Call 01234 567890.

Two things to watch:
- **Length varies.** Longer customer or business names add characters, so check that the longest version still fits within 160.
- **Use plain characters.** Use a straight apostrophe ('), not a curly one (’), and a hyphen (-), not a dash (–). Avoid emoji. Any of those special characters switches the SMS to a different encoding with a **70-character** limit, and the text would then be split into several messages.

## Three checks before handover

1. **Finish and surfaces.** Look for scratches, dents or scuffs from transit, and check that polish or wax hasn't been marked by wrapping or straps.
2. **Moving parts and fittings.** Open and close every drawer and door. Check that handles, hinges and locks work, and hand over any keys.
3. **Stability.** Check that the piece stands level and doesn't rock, and that any parts reassembled on site, such as legs, mirrors or tops, are secure.

It's worth taking a quick photo of each piece once it's in place. Combined with the customer's signature, it settles most disputes later.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?

**Emailed by default.** Capture the signature on a phone or tablet and email the note automatically, ideally with the handover photo attached. It can't be lost, you keep a copy, and it costs nothing. Carry a few paper notes for customers who don't use email or ask for one.

## "Proof of delivery" for your part-timer

**Proof of delivery is a signed and dated record, ideally with a photo, showing that the customer received their item in good condition.**
